lesson.title: Substance P: The Neurotransmitter That Carries Pain
lesson.summary: Substance P is a neuropeptide released by sensory neurons to transmit pain signals into the spinal cord and brain, making it a central chemical messenger for how the nervous system registers injury. It also completes the picture of how endorphins do their job, since they relieve pain largely by suppressing substance P release at its first relay point.
lesson.body:
Not all pain feels the same, and not all of it is carried by the same chemical messenger. The sharp, immediate jolt of stubbing a toe is relayed quickly through fast acting pathways, while the duller, longer lasting ache that follows depends heavily on substance P, a neuropeptide released by sensory neurons that carry information from pain receptors in the skin, joints, and internal organs. Substance P is considered a primary chemical signal for this slower, more persistent quality of pain, the kind that lingers well after the initial injury.

When tissue is damaged, the sensory neurons carrying that pain information release substance P into the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, the first relay station where signals from the body enter the central nervous system proper. There, substance P binds a receptor called the neurokinin-1 (NK1) receptor, which amplifies and prolongs the pain signal as it gets passed further up toward the brain. This amplification is part of what produces sensitization, an increased sensitivity to pain in and around an injured area that can make even mild touch feel uncomfortable for a while after the original damage.

This is also the mechanism that connects directly back to endorphins. Endorphins reduce pain in large part by suppressing the release of substance P at this exact relay point in the spinal cord. When endorphins bind opioid receptors on the terminals of pain sensing neurons, they reduce the calcium influx those terminals need to release their neurotransmitter, so less substance P reaches the dorsal horn and less pain information gets passed along to the brain. Substance P and endorphins are, in effect, opposing forces acting on the very same junction: one turns the pain signal up, the other turns it down.

A useful real world illustration comes from capsaicin, the compound that gives chili peppers their heat. Applied to the skin, capsaicin activates pain sensing neurons and triggers a genuine burning sensation by causing them to release substance P. But with repeated, sustained application, those same neurons gradually deplete their local stores of substance P and become less responsive, an effect that some topical creams exploit deliberately to help manage certain chronic pain conditions, such as the nerve pain that can accompany diabetes, by essentially exhausting the substance P signal in a targeted area over time.

Substance P's reach extends a bit beyond pain as well. It plays a documented role in the nausea and vomiting reflex, which is why drugs that block the NK1 receptor are used clinically as antiemetics for patients undergoing chemotherapy. It has also been investigated as a possible factor in mood and anxiety, though this line of research is considerably less settled, and substance P blocking drugs tested as potential antidepressants have not shown the broad clinical success that was once hoped for, a reminder that a chemical's role in one system, like pain, does not automatically translate into a reliable treatment target in another.
